units.text: Unveiling the disease progression in developmental and epileptic encephalopathies: Insights from EEG and neuropsychology
| INTRODUCTION
2][3] The developmental consequences can be attributed to a combination of the direct effects of the underlying genetic variant and the impact of epileptiform activity.

Patients with DEEs may present with a wide spectrum of symptoms including neurological deficits, intellectual disability, sensory and communication deficits, as well as significant psychiatric, motor, and behavioral disorders. 4,5hese conditions exhibit clinical and genetic heterogeneity, with up to 50% of DEEs attributed to de novo pathogenic variants in single genes, associated with the regulation of neuronal excitability and predominantly encoding synaptic proteins and ion channels. 6,7][12] The clinical course of DEEs has a considerable degree of variability, encompassing a spectrum that ranges from stable conditions to those characterized by progressive neurological decline.

Recently, in a cohort of patients with Dravet syndrome (DS), different neurological and psychiatric deficits have been demonstrated during a 5-year follow-up period including an elevated prevalence of behavioral disorders, specifically attention deficit and autism spectrum symptoms, a decline in language and cognitive functions, as well as numerous neurological examination abnormalities including ataxia and gait abnormalities. 13ollow-up studies on DS investigating long-term outcomes indicate a progressive reduction in epilepsy severity from childhood to adolescence and adulthood. 14onversely, cognitive dysfunction persists into adulthood, irrespective of seizure control, with early-onset seizures correlating with the severity of intellectual disability and language impairment. 15,16oreover, advanced neuroimaging techniques have highlighted the presence of a progressive brain volume reduction in some specific DEEs due to a genetic etiology.

A study on patients diagnosed with CDKL5 deficiency disorder (CDD) using quantitative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed significant reductions in total brain volume and surface area, particularly in the temporal regions, correlating with head circumference. 17atients with DS showed similar reductions in gray and white matter volume and heterogeneous surface area decreases. 18gnificance: Our study provides evidence that a clinical progression may appear in genetic DEEs, manifesting as development or worsening of cognitive impairment and disruption of EEG background activity.These results highlight the challenging clinical course and the importance of early intervention and personalized care in the management of patients with DEEs.
K E Y W O R D S
cognitive impairment, disease progression, drug resistance, EEG, epileptiform abnormalities, genetic DEEs
Key points
• Genetic developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs) are characterized by various seizure types, genetic heterogeneity, and cognitive impairment with variable clinical trajectories.
• Comparison of electroencephalography (EEG)

data between seizure onset and last follow-up revealed a predominance of poorly organized and slow background activity at follow-up.• Cognitive assessments indicated a high prevalence of cognitive impairment, with an increased rate of severe intellectual disability at the last follow-up, highlighting the possible progressive nature of DEEs.• The presence of a high prevalence of drugresistant seizures, status epilepticus, movement disorders, and behavioral problems underscores the need for further research to better understand the complexity underlying DEEs.

MRIs of PCDH19 clustering epilepsy patients revealed reduced cortical gyrification and area, primarily in temporal regions. 19These findings underscore the consistent presence of subtle structural brain alterations in various DEEs, and together with clinical data give insights into a possible progressive course of some DEEs.

The aim of this study is to comprehensively evaluate the clinical progression of a cohort of patients with genetic DEEs by comparing electroencephalography (EEG) and cognitive functions from seizure onset to their last follow-up evaluation.
| METHODS
| Study population

We performed a retrospective analysis on a cohort of 160 patients (94 female) diagnosed with genetic DEEs who were followed up at the epilepsy unit of Bambino Gesù Children's Hospital in Rome, Italy.Patients who were evaluated as second opinions and those without follow-up assessments were excluded from the study cohort.

Genetic variants were identified in all patients through a combination of high-throughput sequencing (exome/ genome/gene panel) and chromosomal microarray for CNV detection.These variants were classified according to American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics guidelines to confirm their alignment with the criteria for being categorized as pathogenic or likely pathogenic. 20ritten informed consent was obtained for research participation and video-EEG recording from all patients, or their parents or legal guardians in the case of minors or adults with intellectual disability.

Considering the retrospective nature of the analysis, the current study did not require the approval of the local ethics committee according to current legislation, but a notification was sent.Data were retrospectively analyzed in line with personal data-protection policies.
| Data collection

We collected clinical data, including gender, genetic variants, age at seizure onset and age at last follow-up, family history, neurological examination, type of seizures at onset, occurrence of febrile seizures at onset, EEG background activity, interictal epileptiform abnormalities, and neuropsychological evaluations.

Furthermore, we investigated additional outcomes at the patients' last follow-up, including presence of drug resistance, occurrence of status epilepticus, seizure frequency and remission, movement disorders, presence of neurological signs, and behavioral problems and/or autism spectrum disorder.
| Definitions and outcomes
We used awake and sleep EEG studies both at onset and follow-up evaluations (not in emergency conditions), with durations ranging from 20 to 30 min to long-term monitoring of 24 to 48 h.
We reviewed all EEG recordings, and we defined background activity as normal, poorly organized and slow, and presence of discontinuous, hypsarrhythmia, and burstsuppression patterns.

We defined EEG background activity as "poorly organized and slow" if characterized by unstructured and undifferentiated brain activity during both wakefulness and sleep, with a predominance of slow wave activity in the delta frequency band, along with the absence of nonrapid eye movement (NREM)-REM differentiation and physiological sleep elements.We grouped epileptiform abnormalities as focal, multifocal, and generalized.The analysis was performed using data from a single EEG control at epilepsy onset and the last EEG at follow-up.

2][23] Status epilepticus was delineated based on the latest definition provided by the ILAE. 24e categorized cognitive evaluations based on total development quotient (DQ) and full-scale intelligence quotient (IQ) and classified them into two primary categories for statistical analysis: normal and abnormal.We kept the same primary categories of normal and abnormal for comparative purposes at both epilepsy onset and at the last follow-up.In addition, we used descriptive statistics to further subcategorize patients with abnormal cognitive functions.
Considering the early age at epilepsy onset, cognitive assessments at first evaluation were categorized into normal and developmental delay based on DQ scores.

At the last follow-up, considering the increased age of the patients and the ability to assess more specific levels of cognitive function, cognitive assessments were grouped based on DQ and IQ scores into normal cognitive function, developmental delay, border intellectual functioning, and mild, moderate, and severe intellectual disability. 25he assessment of cognitive functions in our study was based on categorical variables, which were described using absolute frequencies and percentages.The comparison of cognitive functions between epilepsy onset and the latest follow-up was performed on an individual patient basis.

Developmental and cognitive assessment were performed using the following scales: Griffiths Mental Development Scales-Extended Revised (GMDS-ER), 26 Leiter International Performance Scale-Revised (Leiter-R), 27 Raven's Colored Progressive Matrices (RCPM), Raven's Standard Progressive Matrices (RSPM), 28 Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scale of Intelligence, Third Edition (WPPSI-III), 29 Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children, Fourth Edition (WISC-IV), 30 and Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale, Fourth Edition (WAIS-IV). 31e used the total DQ from the GMDS-ER, the nonverbal IQ score from the Leiter-R, converted percentile ranks to IQ scores for the RCPM and RSPM, and the full-scale IQ scores from the WPPSI-III, WISC-IV, and WAIS-IV to evaluate intellectual functioning.
These assessments were performed by experienced neuropsychologists, and the scores were used to ensure a standardized and reliable classification of cognitive abilities across our patient cohort.

For patients who were unable to complete standardized neuropsychological tests due to a severe phenotype or neonatal seizure onset, cognitive status was determined through a combination of clinical and neurological assessments.This included evaluating developmental milestones as documented in medical records and the clinical judgment of neurologists based on neurological examinations.

We stratified patients according to the number of antiseizure medications (ASMs) they were taking at their last follow-up to assess the potential effects of ASMs on EEG background activity, epileptiform abnormalities, and cognitive functions.The groups were categorized as follows:
(1) no ASMs; (2) monotherapy (1 ASM); (3) 2-3 ASMs; (4) ≥4 ASMs.

We analyzed the total number of ASMs rather than their specific types to assess the medication load, reflecting the cumulative impact of multiple drugs on both EEG and cognitive outcomes.Second, focusing on the number of ASMs can reduce the variability that could arise from the different pharmacological profiles of specific ASMs, providing a more generalized assessment of medication-related effects.

At the last follow-up, we categorized seizure frequency into the following groups: daily (>30 seizure/month), weekly (5-30 seizure/month), monthly (1-4 seizure/ month), sporadic (<1 seizure/month), and remission (seizure absence in the last 2 years).
Moreover, we investigated the presence of movement disorders such as stereotypies, dystonia, chorea, action myoclonus, ataxia, tremor, dyskinesia, and hypokinesia.

In addition, we examined a spectrum of neurological signs, assessing the presence of hypotonia or hypertonia, hemiparesis, tetraparesis, pyramidal and extrapyramidal signs, cerebellar signs, and gait abnormalities.

Behavioral problems and/or autism spectrum disorder were delineated based on a comprehensive assessment, which included personal medical history, clinical observation, administration of semi-structured questionnaires, and through administration of the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule, Second Edition (ADOS-2). 32
| Statistical analysis

Data were analyzed using Statistical Package for Social Sciences SPSS software (version 26.0, Inc., Chicago, Illinois, USA), with descriptive analyses for continuous variables (median and IQR).Categorical variables were presented as absolute number and percentage.Comparison of EEG background activity, epileptiform abnormalities, and cognitive evaluations between seizure onset and last followup evaluation was performed using the McNemar-Bowker test with a significance α level of 5%.

We performed a subgroup analysis of patients with SCN1A variants and those with other pathogenic variants to assess the differences between epilepsy onset and the last follow-up in terms of EEG background activity and cognitive functions.
We used the chi-square test to evaluate the potential impact of ASMs on EEG background activity, epileptiform abnormalities, and cognitive functions at the last follow-up.

We used MATLAB (version R2023b) to generate Sankey diagrams, providing a visual representation of the dynamic changes in EEG background activity, epileptiform abnormalities, and cognitive function from seizure onset to the last follow-up evaluation.
We used the ggplot2 package in R to generate the circular bar plot, illustrating the multi-dimensional interplay of genetic variants, epilepsy syndromes and cognitive functions at last follow-up.
| RESULTS
| Study population
Demographic and clinical characteristics are shown in Table 1.
The median age at seizure onset and the last follow-up was 0.37 (IQR: 0.09-0.75)and 8.54 years (IQR: 4.32-14.55),respectively.
Epilepsy onset with febrile seizures was reported in 23.7% of cases.Furthermore, 60% of patients showed abnormal neurological examination at seizure onset.
We classified seizure types at onset as focal (49.4%), generalized (8.1%), or unknown (42.5%).Twenty-four patients (15%) presented with epileptic spasms at onset.

We investigated potential indicators of disease progression at the last follow-up evaluation, including drug resistance (81.9%), occurrence of status epilepticus (23.1%), movement disorders (60.6%), behavioral problems and autism spectrum disorder (45%), and neurological signs (31.3%).Seizure frequency at the last follow-up visit was daily in 44 patients (27.5%), weekly in 23 (14.4%), monthly in 17 (11.25%),and sporadic in 60 (37.5%).Sixteen patients were in seizure remission at the last follow-up evaluation.
Overall, eight patients died (5%) during the follow-up period due to status epilepticus, sepsis, or neoplasms.
Comparison of EEG background activity, epileptiform abnormalities, and cognitive function at seizure onset and at the last follow-up assessment is illustrated in Table 2.
| EEG

We examined a total of 153 EEG studies at seizure onset.We defined EEG background activity as normal (n = 23; 14.4%); poorly organized and slow (n = 116; 72.5%); and presence of discontinuous, hypsarrhythmia, and burstsuppression patterns (n = 14; 8.8%).
Patients' characteristics

Total number of patients (n = 160)  hypsarrhythmia and burst-suppression patterns (n = 1; 0.6%).We found a statistically significant change in EEG background activity (p = .0017)between seizure onset and the last follow-up: poorly organized and slow background activity increased and presence of discontinuous, hypsarrhythmia, and burst-suppression patterns decreased (Figure 1).
Epileptiform abnormalities at seizure onset were defined as absent (n = 49; 30.6%), focal (n = 49; 30.6%), multifocal (n = 40; 25%), and generalized (n = 15; 9.3%).
At the last follow-up evaluation, epileptiform abnormalities were described as absent (n = 62; 38.8%), focal (n = 47; 29.4%), multifocal (n = 37; 23.1%), and generalized (n = 8; 5%).
We found no statistically significant difference in epileptiform abnormalities (p = .2) between seizure onset and the last follow-up (Figure 2).
| Cognitive functions

Cognitive assessments at seizure onset were performed in 98 patients (61.3%) using the GMDS-ER.For the remaining 62 patients (38.7%) in whom developmental assessment was not feasible due to a severe phenotype or for those characterized by seizure onset during the neonatal period, cognitive evaluation was based on clinical and neurological assessments.

At the last follow-up, a total of 125 patients (78.1%) were assessable, whereas 35 patients (21.9%) were not assessable due to a severe phenotype.The same developmental scale (GMDS-ER) used at seizure onset was administered at the last follow-up evaluation in 25 patients.For the remaining patients, other cognitive tests were used based on their chronological age and the presence or absence of verbal language.Specifically, 44 patients were evaluated using the Leiter-R, 31 patients using RCPM, 15 patients using RSPM, 4 patients using the WPPSI-III, 4 patients using the WISC-IV, and 2 patients using the WAIS-IV.
Cognitive assessments at seizure onset were classified as normal cognitive function (n = 29; 18.1%) and developmental delay (n = 131; 81.9%).

Cognitive assessments at the last follow-up indicated that 151 patients (94.4%) showed cognitive impairment and 9 patients (5.6%) had normal cognitive function (Figure 3).Patients were categorized as developmental delay (n = 19; 12.5%), borderline intellectual functioning (n = 5; 3.1%), mild intellectual disability (n = 18; 11.3%), moderate intellectual disability (n = 34; 21.3%), and severe intellectual disability (n = 74; 46.3%).

A total of nine patients exhibited normal cognitive function both at onset and at the last follow-up evaluation.Of these, six were diagnosed with PCDH19 clustering epilepsy (median age at last follow-up: 3.7 years; median follow-up period: 2.32 years) and showed normal IQ, but were associated with psychiatric comorbidities, including autistic traits, attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder, and aggressive behavior.The remaining three patients were diagnosed with DS (median age at last follow-up: 1.91 years; median follow-up period: 2.56 years).Among these, two had a normal DQ and one had a normal IQ, all associated with behavioral disorders.
There was a significant difference in cognitive function (p = .01)between seizure onset and the last follow-up evaluation with evidence of higher representation of abnormal cognitive function.
| Subgroup analysis of patients with
SCN1A variants and those with other pathogenic variants

We found no statistically significant difference in EEG background activity between epilepsy onset and the last followup in patients with SCN1A variants (p = .454).Conversely, a statistically significant difference was observed in patients with other pathogenic variants (p = .041).

Regarding the analysis of cognitive function, a statistically significant difference was demonstrated for patients with SCN1A variants (p = .000),whereas the difference was not statistically significant in patients with other pathogenic variants (p = .219).
| Antiseizure medications

We categorized patients into four groups based on the number of ASMs they were prescribed at their last follow-up: (1) no ASM, 6 patients; (2) monotherapy, 25 patients; (3) 2-3 ASMs, 92 patients; and (4) ≥4 ASMs: 37 patients.We found no statistically significant differences in EEG background activity (p = .194),epileptiform abnormalities (p = .240),or cognitive function (p = .222)at the last follow-up across the four different groups of patients stratified according to the number of ASMs.
| DISCUSSION

In this retrospective analysis, we examined a cohort of 160 patients with a genetically confirmed diagnosis of DEE.The prevalence of genetic variants varied, with SCN1A being the most commonly identified genetic variant, accounting for 25% of cases (Figure 4).These results underscore the genetic heterogeneity associated with DEEs, which is consistent with the previous literature. 4,11ur analysis of EEG data demonstrated a predominance of poorly organized and slow EEG background activity at seizure onset, accounting for a substantial 72.5% of cases, whereas normal EEG background activity was present in only 14.4% of patients.The presence of EEG disruption since epilepsy onset is consistent with previous studies 33 that have described poorly organized and slow EEG patterns as a common occurrence in patients with severe DEEs.This reflects the underlying changes in cortical connectivity and unstable neural network activity that might be due to the genetic defect regardless of the severity of epilepsy. 34Discontinuous, hypsarrhythmia, and burst-suppression patterns were observed in 8.8% of patients at seizure onset, which may be indicative of a more severe epilepsy phenotype.

However, the most striking finding in our study was the shift in EEG background activity observed during the last follow-up evaluation.At this stage, the prevalence of poorly organized and slow EEG patterns became higher, at 77.5%, consistent with the notion that epilepsy often leads to ongoing disturbances in neural network function. 35,36Nevertheless, we also observed a slight increase in the percentage of patients with normal EEG background activity, rising from 14.4% at seizure onset to 18.1% at the last follow-up, and a reduction of discontinuous, hypsarrhythmia, and burst-suppression patterns to 0.6% of cases.This indicates a potential recovery or stabilization of neural network activity as a result of pharmacological treatment, or it could be indicative of a disease course characterized by a decreasing severity of epilepsy over the years. 14,16,37We recognize that the reduction in the number of individuals with hypsarrhythmia at follow-up is expected, given that initial EEG recordings were obtained in infancy when hypsarrhythmia is more prevalent, and that subsequent EEG recordings were obtained in older children, in whom hypsarrhythmia often evolves into different patterns.In some conditions, however, this pattern may persist beyond infancy, such as in severe DEEs, inadequate treatment, underlying genetic or metabolic disorders, structural brain abnormalities.The observed reduction in hypsarrhythmia reflects the natural progression of EEG patterns within the studied age range of patients with DEEs.Retained hypsarrhythmia at follow-up is rare, and its reduction over time is a well-documented phenomenon, indicating an age-related progression rather than an unexpected improvement.

Although we did not observe significant differences in the prevalence of epileptiform abnormalities between seizure onset and the most recent follow-up, a proportion of patients (38.8%) exhibited no detectable epileptiform abnormalities.However, considering the heterogeneity of etiologies and the limited amount of EEG data, the possibility of spontaneous fluctuations or stochastic effects of ASMs cannot be excluded.

This observation is promising, as it points to the possibility of achieving better control over epileptic activity through medical interventions and management strategies. 38It also raises questions about the mechanisms behind the resolution or reduction of epileptiform abnormalities, which should be further explored.

We detected a significant shift in cognitive functions, with a high prevalence of cognitive impairment at the last follow-up.At seizure onset, our findings indicated that the majority of patients (81.9%) presented with cognitive abnormal findings, whereas only a minority (18.1%) exhibited normal cognitive function.The notable shift in cognitive functioning was evident when comparing cognitive assessments at the last follow-up evaluation which documented an increase of patients with abnormal cognitive function.The spectrum of cognitive impairments also widened, with some patients moving from developmental delay to more severe categories of intellectual disability.The observed widening of the spectrum of cognitive impairments reflects the detailed categorization process at the follow-up stage, made possible by the increased age of the participants and the corresponding ability to assess more specific levels of cognitive function.

Regarding the reduction in the number of patients demonstrating normal development from onset to the last assessment, it is relevant to consider that this trend may be an expression of developmental regression, characterized by the loss of previously acquired developmental skills or abilities over time.Alternatively, it could be attributed to stagnation, which refers to the absence of expected progress in cognitive or developmental milestones compared to typical developmental trajectories.

Furthermore, a significant increase in the proportion of patients with severe intellectual disability was observed, highlighting the cognitive regression that often accompanies DEEs. 16,39,40his finding is consistent with the progressive nature of DEEs and underscores the need for early and ongoing cognitive support and intervention for affected individuals. 41ithin the subgroup of patients who maintained normal cognitive function at the last follow-up, were included patients with PCDH19 clustering epilepsy (where it is expected that about 30% of patients present normal cognitive outcome) and patients with DS during the earlier stage of disease.

Consequently, we included these patients according to the ILAE definition, recognizing that there are instances where patients may demonstrate normal cognitive function at an early stage of the disease, which may subsequently deteriorate with a longer follow-up period.This inclusion is consistent with the understanding that DEEs encompass a broad spectrum of cognitive outcomes, and that early normal cognition does not preclude the possibility of later cognitive decline or the presence of significant psychiatric comorbidities.

Conversely, it is important to consider that a significant proportion of patients within this cohort may initially present with a severe phenotype.This characteristic could pose challenges in accurately assessing clinical deterioration over time.The inherent severity bias at baseline may introduce complexities in evaluating potential clinical improvement, even if it exists, and could complicate the interpretation of longitudinal outcomes at the last follow-up evaluation.

The findings of our study indicate that the number of ASMs does not influence EEG background activity and appears not to significantly affect epileptiform abnormalities and cognitive function.The majority of patients exhibit impaired cognitive outcomes and poorly organized and slow EEG background activity at the last follow-up, irrespective of the number of ASMs administered.

Notably, a substantial number of patients exhibited drug-resistant seizures, emphasizing the challenges in managing DEEs, and highlights the need for innovative treatment approaches to enhance seizure control. 38,42,43uch high rates of drug resistance have been documented in other studies, emphasizing the refractory nature of DEE. 44,45The occurrence of status epilepticus was observed in approximately one fourth of the patients, highlighting the urgency and complexity of seizure control in this population.Status epilepticus is associated with high morbidity and mortality, making its occurrence in a significant proportion of patients with DEE a matter of great concern. 46ur study also revealed a high frequency of movement disorders (60.6%) and behavioral and autism spectrum disorder (45%) among patients with DEE.A growing body of literature recognizes the co-occurrence of movement disorders in patients with DEE, pointing out the importance of a comprehensive clinical assessment and intervention. 47,48pilepsy in DEE is characterized often by intractable seizures resulting from various dysfunctions in neuronal activity.It is well known that epilepsy is associated wtih various changes in neuronal structure, including processes such as apoptosis, dendritic growth, synaptic remodeling, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation. 49Overall these changes might reflect reductions in dendritic arborization and be responsible for a progressive reduction in brain cortical volume, 50 determining a progressive course in such conditions.

In light of the considerations deriving from the present study and pre-clinical studies, regarding the possible progressive nature of genetic DEEs, we think that the past approach whereby progression was considered a typical characteristic of metabolic diseases should now be reassessed.This is because even genetic DEEs, which are non-metabolic but involve pathways related to processes such as apoptosis, dendritic growth, synaptic remodeling, oxidative stress, and neuroinflammation, may cause neurodegeneration.

This insight underscores the importance of early and targeted intervention and the need for treatments that address the multifaceted nature of these conditions, aiming to control seizures and reduce pathological changes in neuronal functions and structures to slow the disease's progression.

Although DEEs manifest with a wide range of symptoms and severities, this study provides compelling evidence that for many patients, DEEs are progressive conditions.The ongoing epileptic activity, cognitive regression, and persistent or worsening clinical symptoms underscore the need for innovative treatment strategies and comprehensive care approaches aimed at mitigating the progression of these debilitating disorders.The absence of MRI data limits our ability to comprehensively assess the progressive nature of DEEs in the provided article; integrating neuroimaging findings into future studies could enhance our understanding of the underlying pathophysiology and inform clinical management strategies for patients with these complex neurological disorders.
| Limitations

Although this study provides valuable insights into the clinical progression in patients with DEEs, it is important to acknowledge several limitations that may impact the interpretation of the results.

We performed a retrospective study, relying on the analysis of historical data.This design inherently introduces potential biases related to data collection, selection of patients, and the completeness of medical records.The study focused on a cohort of 160 patients from a single epilepsy center, which may not be representative of the entire DEE population.The findings may not be directly generalizable to broader or more diverse patient groups.

In addition, the discrepancy in cognitive follow-up assessments complicates longitudinal comparisons and may affect the reliability of monitoring cognitive changes over time, making it challenging to directly compare results across the entire patient cohort.

The predominance of SCN1A variants in our cohort may have influenced the results, as 40 individuals with SCN1A variants represent a significant portion of the study population (25%).This substantial representation could distort the findings, particularly the observed progression of cognitive delay, given the well-documented developmental regression associated with SCN1A-related disorders.In addition, conducting a gene-by-gene analysis was limited by the small sample sizes for many of the other individual genetic variants.Grouping the data into subcategories based on gene mechanisms was also challenging due to the diverse and heterogeneous nature of the DEEs.Consequently, although our study provides a comprehensive description of DEEs as a whole, the impact of SCN1A variants must be considered carefully when interpreting the results.Therefore, concluding that DEEs as a general category exhibit a progressive nature may not be entirely accurate without considering these genotype-specific variations.

This study lacks a control group for comparative analysis, making it challenging to differentiate between the natural progression of DEEs and potential treatment effects, as well as to account for external factors that may influence the observed outcomes.

It is plausible that specific genetic etiologies are more closely correlated with disease progression, with specific genes or pathogenic pathways being implicated.This analysis was not performed due to the considerable genetic variability present in our cohort.It should be taken into consideration that not all DEEs have the same rate of progression and it is the underlying genetic factor that primarily drives the disease progression.
| CONCLUSION

This represents the first study that has assessed the potential existence of disease progression in a heterogeneous cohort of patients with DEEs, by evaluating clinical, EEG, and neuropsychological data.Overall, our study provides valuable insights into the clinical course and characteristics of DEEs, showing the complex interplay of genetic, clinical, and cognitive factors.The progressive nature of DEEs underscores the importance of early diagnosis and intervention, and our findings emphasize the need for a multidisciplinary approach to the management of DEE patients, including personalized treatments, cognitive support, and close monitoring of seizure activity.

Investigating DEEs as a comprehensive entity rather than on a gene-by-gene basis offers several advantages.First, studying DEEs as a whole is resource efficient.Given the large number of patients with DEEs without a definitive genetic cause despite extensive testing, a comprehensive evaluation of patients may uncover patterns that may be missed in a fragmented gene-by-gene analysis.Furthermore, the overlapping phenotypes observed in DEEs suggest the potential for shared pathogenic mechanisms, enabling the identification of common pathways and the development of targeted therapies that could benefit a broader patient population.

In addition, this holistic approach can promote the development of more effective diagnostic strategies.Understanding the broader genetic and phenotypic landscape of DEEs enhances our ability to identify diagnostic markers and predict disease progression.This leads to the development of more robust diagnostic tools, facilitating earlier and more accurate diagnosis for patients.

Further research is needed to explore the underlying mechanisms of disease progression in DEEs, as well as to evaluate the long-term outcomes of different treatment strategies.Furthermore, multicenter prospective studies with larger and more heterogenous patient populations are needed to enhance the external validity of these findings, overcoming some of these limitations, and to provide a more robust understanding of DEEs and their clinical progression.
